I haven't seen The Housemaid by the same director and I think that's a bit of a problem as this is a heavily stylised and hysterically acted variation on the film he laid down over a decade earlier. Everything here has a melodrama turned up to the highest settings and the cast's performances become so flailing and ridiculous that you wonder if the film is insisting on not being taken seriously. What's more most of the cool stylisation is really front loaded and that's before the dialogue completely goes to crazy town so you're left with a first half that routinely looks really interesting and a tone which is off-kilter but not completely lost and then a second half where people are just having wild emotional swings and routinely falling in to complete hysteria in sets you've now seen a dozen times with lighting that can only be described as generic. The final sequence with two of the characters still manipulating future events whilst dying from having ingested rat poison did win me back a bit though. I'm still sat here having no clue what the film was even trying to do which makes critiquing it quite hard. Freya's rating: 1/5

«Женщина в огне» – первый авторемейк эпохальной «Горничной» Ким Ги-ёна (второй выйдет спустя одиннадцать лет), своеобразная ревизия общественных нравов, выполняемая режиссером раз в десятилетие. Для корейских кинематографистов «Hanyo» стала настольной библией, а ее сюжет стал бродячим, плотно войдя в кинематографический канон. Новая версия культовой картины, вошедшая в мизогиническую трилогию, очевидно, снята под большим влиянием джалло, в отличие от строгого по форме черно-белого оригинала первый авторемейк изобилует всеми оттенками взрывных красного и синего, а квартирные интерьеры становятся объектом эстетизации. Ким Ги-ён или как его прозвали на родине «господин Монстр» выходит на пик своей творческой формы, снимая предельно экзальтированные картины, смешивающие особенности корейского менталитета, насилие, разрушение семьи, сексуальные девиации, женобоязнь и дикие сюрреалистические образы. В «Hwanyeo» режиссер немного отходит в сторону от социальных аллегорий оригинала, делая акцент на психологической подоплеке поступков героев – они идут вразнос, чтобы постепенно сойти с ума. С наступлением Четвертой республики в стране уже установилась цензура, поэтому кореец выбирает самое надежное укрытие – в глубине жанровых картин, но его персонажи по-прежнему зловещи и пугающи, балансируя на грани откровенной карикатуры и звериной монструозности. Дебютантка Юн Ё-Дзён, сыгравшая коварную деревенскую простушку, открыла галерею чудовищ в женском обличье в самом ярком творческом десятилетии режиссера, но в отличие от злодейки из первого фильма, поступки героини, выбравшей проторить себе путь наверх по социальной лестнице, обоснованы ненавистью в сторону мира мужчин, уже жестоко обошедшегося с девушкой. Ким Ги-ён вставляет в самые кульминационные моменты звук удара по раскаленному железу (постоянно напоминающий героине о чудовищном моменте из прошлого), вместе с кислотной цветовой палитрой и чередой взрывных экспрессионистских образов они окаймляют психологические перверсии, разрушающие шаткий мир корейской семьи, свято чтящей патриархат и встроенной в жесткое капиталистическое общество. Колесо смерти набирает обороты, руки героев окрашиваются кровью, безумие уже замерло на пороге. Новая версия классовой «Служанки» мутирует в психоделическую мелодраму о женщинах и мужчинах на грани нервного срыва, незваная гостья, обуреваемая стыдом и желанием, преследуемая психологической травмой, срывает маски с благопристойных членов корейского общества, как огня боящихся разоблачения и потери статуса. Если в оригинале Ким Ги-ён выводил на экране кровожадных паучих, рвущих мужчину на части, чтобы сделать его марионеткой в своих руках, то в «Женщина в огне» превращает героиню в разносящую по дому заразу крысу, искажая внутренний мир хозяев дома, забывающих о всех моральных ценностях и превращающихся в зверей. В картине есть как грех, так и искупление, как похоть, так и невинность, как отчаяние, так и смирение. Но благообразная маска успешной семьи, чей социальный капитал гораздо важнее любви и преданности, уже треснула, поэтому вой оставшейся в живых перебивает звон ненавистного металла. Грязное, извращенное и одновременно притягивающее к себе зрелище.

First remake of the original film The Housemaid by the same director a decade later.  This one has a similar cadence but the garish color palette is vastly different from the original black and white.  The menace of the mistress happens sooner and more obviously in this version. The seduction of the husband has a very similar feeling of inevitability, as if everyone is powerless to stop it. The other added element here is the police investigation that starts the film with a double murder. And of course a staircase and rats once again plays a central role in the story as well.

Performances are so hammy and overdone (which I fully believe is intentional) that I think it undermines the visual flourishes. IMO, inserting still-image montage, subjective techniques, jarring color choices into an otherwise more subdued narrative style is more interesting. What Kim Ki-young does here makes the melodramatic scenes feel flattened. Idk if there's truly anything new here, and tbh I think I prefer the abject misery and disjoint of INSECT WOMAN. Still very fascinating that Kim Ki-young made a masterpiece in 1960 and spent his career trying to remake the same story (often with the same actors).

If The Housemaid 's bleak depiction of economic strife and moral complexities came with the danger of dehumanising its crazed villainess a little bit, Kim Ki-young's remake of his own film a decade later rectifies this. Although she also goes off the deep end later in the film, Myeong-ja starts out a much more sympathetic character, and the film is overall told from a more female perspective. It's still the second time we've seen this story play out, and the change of perspective doesn't completely hide the sense of familiarity. There's some stylish colour play going on, the shot compositions are also very well chosen, and Youn Yuh-jung is fantastic, but it doesn't pack the surprising punch that the original did. I should probably mention that I watched the French-subtitled version on YouTube, so some subtleties may have been lost on me.

IF you have seen any thriller film you know what is going to happen and if like me, you saw the first film then you pretty much know the whole film from the start to finish. Forgive my getting all anachronistic and Western, but I had The Cult stuck in my head throughout the movie. The poster does suggest that this is just a zestier "The Housemaid", because it's not like relocating to a remote place where they slaughter critters will lighten the tension. Sure enough, we open on Namkoong Won's Dong-shik murdered, but alongside Youn Yuh-jung's Myeong-ja, his farm hand. The police suspect the wife, Jeon Gye-hyeon's Jeong-suk, only to discover a letter written by the female victim that could hold the answers. We flash back to Meyong-ja coming to Jeong-suk's struggling family farmhouse, who agrees to work for free in order to cope with the trauma that drove her from these parts. She and the songwriter Dong-shik end up developing a mutual attraction, but as this takes several tragic turns, Jeong-suk becomes deathly dedicated to taking revenge on this family. She's a rising fire alright, Ian Astbury, but the film works a little too hard to go more highbrow. The spiritual successor to the unlikely classic "The Housemaid" is similarly, audaciously melodramatic, with thematic and moral complications that could exceed the original. But if you're going in expecting the usual trashy fun with a married couple and a temptress in a homicidal ménage à Troi, expect to be deeply disturbed and depressed by the turns this takes. Still, this boasts all the over-the-top style and brash musical stinging of the trashiest of soap operas, unwinding the finer points of dramatic storytelling. That does of course include labored pacing and convoluted nonlinear structuring to extend the dimensions of the characters and their bleak predicaments. It may be futile, as broad as the writing is long before it shifts the characters in such drastically dark directions that evolution to that point doesn't quite add up. Neither does the logic of situations that often bend to the bleakness, as well as many of the trappings of "The Housemaid", with a lot less tonal tact. This is just a monotonously morose melodrama, but does indeed aim higher than the trashiness. The likes of Jung Il-sung's vibrant, dynamic cinematography and Han Sang-ki's striking score do hit that sweet spot between the trash and the prestige. Kim Ki-young's direction merely abuses these artistic endeavors, with sensational extremes that more-or-less work with escalations in erotic or violent thrills. I for one found it much more engaging for him to play with the scarlet lighting and dizzying filming of this gorgeous, claustrophobic farmhouse, as a means of establishing and evolving psychological tension. Underlying that more intelligent tension is a sleazy erotic and revenge thriller that will definitely keep you on your toes with its depressing extremes, when it wants to say more. It actually says more about the complicated role of women in this gruesome power play, with their resilience in the face of trauma and exploitation, until they explode in a way that consumes the complacent and the innocent alike. Namkoong Won's intensity may be the right mix of pathetic tragic figure and absolute monster, but Jeon Gye-hyeon and Youn Yuh-jung are real forces of tortured menace that often just breaks your heart. There is taste and talent at hand, but both are wasted by excess, and the wrong sort of it. As the melodrama goes increasingly brutal, the manipulatively overwrought direction and tricky structure further cheapen a tension well-founded by more psychological and visceral characterization, while saucy allegories and acting narrowly raise Kim Ki-young's "Fire Woman"-I mean "Woman of Fi-aaahhh-ah-ah-ah-ah-re" out of its burnout as a searing, sensually grim battle of the sexes. 3/5 - Decent

Woman of Fire | Kim Ki-young | 1971 | 2024 Asian Cinema Season - Film 130 "You may have taken my life but my soul... I cannot give it to you." Kim Ki-young’s Woman of Fire (1971) reimagines his earlier film The Housemaid (1960) with a continued focus on class, gender, and the darker aspects of human nature. The film tells the story of Myeong-Ja, a young woman from the countryside who becomes a maid for the Dong-Sik family in Seoul. Her presence disrupts the family’s stability, revealing the underlying tensions and hypocrisies of their lives. Myeong-Ja is not just a disruptor but a symbol of the hidden forces within society that challenge the status quo. Her actions expose the vulnerabilities and pretences of the Dong-Sik family, highlighting the personal conflicts and moral decay in their household. The transition from rural to urban life, depicted through Myeong-Ja’s journey, reflects her struggle and the shifting dynamics within the family. "When you autopsy human nature, black blood will flow out. That is what we call desire." – Kim Ki-young The film critiques the patriarchal and hierarchical structures of the family. The male characters, though outwardly powerful, are often weak and morally corrupt. Dong-Sik, the husband, succumbs to a destructive affair with Myeong-Ja, symbolising his moral decay and the fragility of his authority. His affair with Myeong-Ja is a catalyst that brings to light the suppressed desires and frustrations within the household. What drives a person to abandon their moral compass for fleeting desires? The use of colour, especially reds and blues, symbolises the intense emotions and tensions within the household. Red, in particular, points to passion, violence, and the blood ties that bind and destroy the characters. This vivid use of colour heightens the film’s dramatic impact, making it a visual spectacle that draws the audience into its emotional core. One of the film's most compelling aspects is its portrayal of women. Myeong-Ja, initially a victim of her circumstances, evolves into a powerful figure who challenges the established order. Her actions force the other characters, and the audience, to confront uncomfortable truths about gender roles and societal expectations. How far will someone go to assert their agency in a world that seeks to suppress them? The film was released during a time of significant political and social change in South Korea. Censorship was rife, and filmmakers had to navigate these restrictions carefully. Kim Ki-young cleverly uses visual metaphors and indirect storytelling to bypass censorship, allowing him to explore provocative themes without explicit content. Scenes of sexual tension and violence are often depicted through shadows, reflections, and suggestive imagery, enhancing the film’s psychological impact while complying with censorship laws. Woman of Fire also explores themes of power and control within the intimate setting of the household. The Dong-Sik family’s attempt to maintain their social status and control over their environment ultimately leads to their downfall. This internal struggle reflects the broader societal tensions of maintaining appearances versus confronting hidden truths. While Woman of Fire is a powerful and significant work in its own right, it is perhaps somewhat derivative of Kim's earlier film, The Housemaid. The core narrative and thematic elements are revisited and expanded upon, which might make the film feel familiar to those who have seen the original. However, this does not diminish the film’s impact; instead, it offers a deeper, more stylised exploration of similar themes. The film can be seen as an evolution of Kim's ideas, where he refines his critique of societal norms and human desires. In my view, Woman of Fire stands out for its thematic depth and historical relevance. Kim Ki-young dissects societal structures with a keen eye, presenting a narrative that explores the complexities of human nature. The film's ability to provoke thought and challenge perceptions makes it a powerful piece of cinema that continues to resonate with audiences today. Its influence is evident in contemporary Korean cinema, inspiring films like Parasite that similarly critique social hierarchies and human desires.

This was her debut performance, and it has to be said that it shows: she has this habit of jutting out her teeth in every reaction shot, and it’s distracting as hell. Youn has said that she didn’t enjoy working with Kim, and on the evidence it’s easy to see why: he treats the actors less like people than as vessels for the projection of his ideas. With this semi-remake of The Housemaid , it’s almost as if he set out to recreate that film in crash course form. His obsessions coalesce into florid extremities, whereas the brutally compressed plot beats make little sense without the context of the earlier counterpart. For something so drenched in arch style, I think the most impactful and memorable moment is, ironically, the final scene: an unvarnished outpouring of emotion, heightened by the stark use of white. Directors who remake their own movies is a bit of a mixed bag.  Sometimes it’s simply anglicizing a foreign language success for US audiences ( The Vanishing, Gloria Bell, Funny Games ), a director embracing technological advances in use of colour ( Floating Weeds, Good Morning, The Man Who Knew Too Much, Kismet ), the recognition of changing mores/or censorship (the These Three love triangle gets a same sex update with The Children’s Hour ), a shift in genre ( High Sierra becomes a Western with Colorado Territory , comedies like Ball of Fire & The Strawberry Blonde become musicals with A Song is Born & One Wonderful Sunday ), or sometimes a director is in cruise control run out of ideas (see Frank Capra with late period stuff like Riding High and Pocketful of Miracles ). With this Korean film, Kim Ki-young remakes his legendary cautionary melodrama/thriller The Housemaid (1960) and the post-new wave stylistic updates are wild - ‘scope framing with off-kilter compositions, vivid expressive colour, and experimental still frame shock cuts.  While the original was really more pulp than art house (despite some fluid camera moves seemingly out of Max Ophüls) Kim Ki-young doubles down on the kooky and lurid plot turns (and the chicken farm setting might suggest the giallo adjacent Italian mystery/horror Death Laid an Egg ). Bonkers in the most compelling way - right there with the other East Asian envelope pushing genre films of the era.

The second version of The Housemaid that Kim Ki-young made, the notable difference being that it was filmed in colour. And when I say colour, I really mean it- this is one of the most lurid Korean films of the period, a relentless assault of red, purple and yellow. Before his critical reassessment in the 90s, this excessive quality in the Kim’s work won him a reputation among Korean cinephiles as a sort of Ed Wood figure- unfairly so, because he was clearly a technically accomplished helmsman. What lets him down is the narrative, where he repeats the same mistake he made in the original. Although the maid is given a fleshed out backstory, her descent into evil is barely developed, and she comes across as a figment of Kim’s most misogynistic nightmares more than anything else. So while there is, undeniably, something to this story- so much so that Kim returned to it three more times- Bong Joon-ho was doing himself a disservice when he compared Parasite to Kim’s oeuvre. Even at its most affecting, there is a sense that Fire Woman is made by a director who can’t quite control his own compulsions. Kim Ki-young's Housemaid (1961) frequently has "best Korean film" praise thrown at it - a predecessor to the erotic thriller, about the title character bringing a family to ruin.  The runaway success meant that Kim would revisit the collateral damage of extramarital affairs for a "Housemaid Trilogy" - while making a number of other efforts in a very similar vein (i.e. Insect Woman).  Woman of Fire (1971) is the second film in the trilogy, and features Oscar winner Youn Yuh-jung (Minari) in her feature film debut, as our femme fatale homewrecker.  This is not a spiritual sequel, but rather the director remaking his work a decade later. Woman of Fire streamlines the narrative, cutting down on the family dynamic, now primarily taking the perspective of the Housemaid.  The children are non-characters, which removes a vulnerability that drove the originals abstract terror, and made it so perversely compelling.  Instead the extra minutes not dedicated to similar beats and exactly the same dialogue, have a more elaborate blackmail set-up, and three sexual assaults.  It's rougher and more graphic, sadly losing the cerebral aspects that made the original so steeped in dread & unique.  The decision to revisit the work in decade cycles, is an interesting one - as the world has changed drastically in ten years.  A big part of the 1961 situation was economic factors forcing the nuclear family into an impossible situation, here the threat of financial ruin no longer holds sway - and ease with which the husband is seduced makes him comedically buffoonish.  The architecture of the house is delightful, with sharp features inviting the Dutch camera angles that follow.  Now in colour, with Kim making the most of them - frequently saturate the image in reds and blues that lend themselves to the fever dream asthetic.  Experimental editing abounds, with the death of an infant handled in a tasteful succession of still images.  While the narrative asks less of the audience, and characters, it is still grounded in two powerhouse performances by Youn, and Jeon Gye-hyeon as the wife. Worth seeking out, and I would strongly encourage viewing it as a double bill with the original for insights into the changing times, and evolution of the artists' choices in a much stricter environment. A (far) superior iteration on Kim’s better-known The Housemaid (1960), bolstered by a visual palette that vacillates between giallo and Sirk. The evocation of the former makes sense given the film’s pulpy preoccupations, but the echoes of the latter—the deep blues and reds, the mediated shots through windows—in the film’s cinematography feels like it hints at Kim’s less overt but no less central social preoccupations: The imprisonment his characters endure due to entrenched social norms, and all that they willing to do to (or deny of) themselves and each other to preserve some nebulous sense of honor. There is also maybe a little bit here about what it’s like to make art under such oppressive and stifling societal contexts. It doesn’t feel unintentional that the meat grinder—which turns bones and meat into chicken feed—looks like a film camera. Excellent. Kind of reminds me of Insiang.

This month I've been exploring South Korean cinema, so I watched The Housemaid (1960) and every bit of praise I'd read made sense. A highly sexual domestic horror shot in striking black and white with endless storms outside. It's clear why it is considered so important. The kind of film that gets under your skin. Fire Woman is director Kim Ki-young remaking that earlier film of his by turning it into an almost psychedelic nightmare with unnatural colours, carefully constructed sets designed to obscure eroticism and violence, and furiously edited flashes of disturbing images in moments of intensity. From the very start you know that something horrible is going to happen, it's not a subtle film when it comes to how the plot is laid out. Scenes from a murder investigation are weaved in and out. It's also every bit as good as The Housemaid. Youn Yuh-jung as the young maid is a more sympathetic figure initially than the maid in the original film, she seems to narrowly avoid being exploited and appears more naive. She also has this odd way of smiling that would put fear into anyone. Something like that, a small visible part of her character is a tease for the advertised madness. It's one of those stories where everyone is so desperate to come out on top that there is ultimately no one to root for or who looks good.
